CDC-02-SE-03: Smiling/talking with familiar people does not require a happy reaction when someone approaches.
CDC-02-LC-01: Vowel cooing and guttural syllables are specific vocal forms; the broader any-noncry-sound threshold is not separately asked.
CDC-02-CO-02: Kinedu requires one minute of attention, rather than several seconds looking at a toy.
CDC-02-MP-02: Separate arm and leg items do not require movement of both arms and both legs in one question.
CDC-02-MP-03: Palm-touch-elicited opening and closing is a different task from briefly opening the hands.
CDC-04-SE-01: A responsive eye-contact smile or a generic attention bid does not establish a spontaneous attention-seeking smile.
CDC-04-SE-02: Laughing out loud is a higher threshold than CDC's explicitly not-yet-full chuckle; paired with the six-month laugh instead.
CDC-04-LC-02: Responding with babbles has the same conversational function, but babbling may require a harder vocal form than CDC's unspecified sounds. The level cannot be equated strictly.
CDC-04-LC-03: Looking toward a noise does not specify a head turn toward a person's voice.
CDC-04-CO-01: No question specifies opening the mouth on seeing breast or bottle when hungry.
CDC-04-MP-01: Holding the head up without a specified posture is ambiguous; the other items add standing torso control or still require support.
CDC-04-MP-03: Reaching and grasping is a more directed action than swinging the arm at a toy.
CDC-06-SE-02: Reacting to a reflection does not establish liking to look; recognizing oneself is a different, more advanced claim.
CDC-06-LC-01: Both involve vocal turn-taking, but Kinedu specifies babbling rather than any sounds. Whether that adds a phonological requirement is unknown; excluded conservatively.
CDC-06-LC-03: No squealing question; general babbling does not specify squeals.
CDC-06-MP-02: Lifting the upper body or extending arms forward does not specify weight-bearing on straight arms.
CDC-09-SE-02: Likes/dislikes expressed facially do not establish CDC's wider set of several expressions.
CDC-09-SE-05: Enjoying adult play or laughing generally does not specify peek-a-boo.
CDC-09-MP-03: Holding an object with the fingers is not the finger-raking motion that brings food toward the child.
CDC-12-SE-01: Enjoying play or copying a clapping gesture does not require reciprocal games such as pat-a-cake.
CDC-12-MP-03: General correct cup/item use omits adult holding and lid status; one-handed drinking adds a different motor requirement.
CDC-15-SE-02: Pointing to show is a different gesture from showing an object; the pointing question is paired with CDC's eighteen-month pointing item.
CDC-15-SE-03: Imitating clapping or keeping a beat does not establish spontaneous clapping when excited.
CDC-15-SE-04: Affection to people and pretending to feed a doll do not require hugging a toy.
CDC-15-LC-01: At least one meaningful word can include a parent name; Kinedu does not state CDC's besides-mama/dada exclusion.
CDC-15-LC-03: Giving an object on request/one-step instructions leave gesture support unspecified; CDC explicitly provides both a gesture and words.
CDC-15-CO-01: Can correctly use everyday items is a success criterion; CDC only requires trying to use them appropriately.
CDC-15-MP-02: Independent feeding with or without utensils does not establish feeding with fingers specifically.
CDC-18-SE-01: Exploration near a caregiver omits looking back to check the caregiver's location.
CDC-18-SE-04: Sustained attention for a few minutes while an adult reads is not the same minimal shared-looking-at-a-few-pages threshold.
CDC-18-LC-01: Four words total or three named objects do not unambiguously require three words besides parent names.
CDC-18-LC-02: Kinedu does not explicitly rule out gesture cues; CDC's no-gesture requirement materially affects difficulty.
CDC-18-CO-01: Helping with chores need not be imitation; general family imitation need not involve chores.
CDC-18-MP-01: A few first unsteady steps are earlier than established walking; walking while carrying a toy adds a task. No plain sustained-walking counterpart.
CDC-18-MP-03: One-handed cup drinking adds a motor constraint; general everyday-item use omits the open-cup and assistance conditions.
CDC-18-MP-04: The question permits utensil feeding and does not require fingers.
CDC-18-MP-05: Independent successful spoon use is harder than trying; paired with CDC's two-year spoon-eating item instead.
CDC-18-MP-06: Sitting in a small chair or climbing generally does not require independently climbing both on and off furniture.
CDC-24-SE-01: Actively comforting an upset person is a higher threshold than merely noticing; paired with CDC's four-year comforting item.
CDC-24-SE-02: Looking at faces does not establish using another person's expression to guide a response to a new situation.
CDC-24-LC-01: Matching items to pictures or identifying story characters omits the requested pointing response to a named book picture.
CDC-24-LC-03: One pointed body part is too few; naming three or smaller parts uses a different response and higher threshold.
CDC-24-LC-04: Gesture imitation can be only waves/points; CDC requires additional communicative gestures.
CDC-24-CO-03: Pretend feeding does not explicitly require coordinating two toys; neither question specifies CDC's multi-toy action.
CDC-24-MP-02: Similar-to-running acceleration is ambiguous; directed running or confident running across surfaces adds requirements.
CDC-24-MP-03: Alternating feet or no hand support is harder; crawling stairs is a different action. No basic stair-walking question at the same level.
CDC-30-SE-01: Parallel play explicitly without interaction misses sometimes playing together; general social play omits the combined pattern.
CDC-30-SE-02: Attention-seeking sounds/actions do not require verbally showing one's achievement with a look-at-me statement.
CDC-30-SE-03: Chore participation or rule understanding does not require following a familiar routine after a spoken cue.
CDC-30-LC-03: Naming familiar/everyday objects does not specify naming a book picture after a pointed what-is-this prompt.
CDC-30-CO-01: Generic make-believe, feeding a doll, or making toys talk does not require object substitution, such as a block standing for food.
CDC-30-CO-02: Moving an obstacle to reach something is not the same means-to-an-end level as using a stool/tool to extend one's reach.
CDC-36-SE-01: Calming to a voice does not require independent recovery within ten minutes after separation.
CDC-36-SE-02: Enjoying/prefering play with peers does not explicitly require noticing and joining them.
CDC-36-LC-01: A count of sentences is not a count of reciprocal conversational exchanges; the turn-taking threshold is unspecified.
CDC-36-LC-02: Answering who/what/where questions is a different behavior from asking them.
CDC-36-LC-03: Receptively understanding action words is different from expressively naming a pictured action.
CDC-36-LC-04: Name plus age/gender or first-and-last name adds requirements to CDC's first name alone.
CDC-36-CO-01: Circular scribbling does not require an intentional closed circle copied after demonstration.
CDC-36-CO-02: Reacting differently to hot/cold things does not require avoiding a hot object after a warning.
CDC-48-SE-02: Preferring peers or naming friends does not require asking to play with an absent child.
CDC-48-SE-04: No danger-avoidance question at this level.
CDC-48-SE-05: Actually helping with chores does not specifically measure liking the helper role.
CDC-48-SE-06: Adjusting voice volume is one narrow part of behavior; the question does not require broader setting-dependent behavior.
CDC-48-LC-04: Knowing body-part functions or answering a color question does not ask about everyday objects' purposes.
CDC-48-CO-02: Filling a familiar line's blank or recalling yesterday's story does not necessarily predict the next event in a known story.
CDC-48-CO-03: Naming/describing a drawing does not require a person with three body parts.
CDC-48-MP-01: Catching a large ball while steady, hands-only catching, or catching a bounced ball does not establish CDC's most-of-the-time reliability at the same task.
CDC-48-MP-04: A whole-hand crayon grip is the opposite of CDC's specified finger-and-thumb grip.
